When the node stops answering for 5 minutes, the app writes a report and restarts the node, up to 3 times in 6 hours.

A report shows what each part of the node was doing (its goroutines) and about the last 20 minutes of its log. It holds the node's address and its peers' network addresses, no key.

If your node has trouble connecting or syncing: Make a report, Save the last report, and share it with the Idena community to understand what happens.
The node made no report: is it running?
The node takes these at its next start:
A restart now takes a few minutes: the node opens its databases and looks for peers again.

How many Idena nodes the phone stays connected to. Blocks, votes and transactions come from them.

Eco: up to %1$d. Less data and battery, but after a network drop the node can take longer to find peers again.

Normal (default): up to %2$d, as on a computer.

Hub: up to %3$d, with more room for nodes that connect to the phone. It helps only when nodes outside can reach the phone (a port open on the router). More data and battery: best on Wi-Fi and while charging.

The node takes the level at its start.

IPFS connections carry flips, posts and the records that tell which node has them. The node finds its Idena peers among them.

Above the limit the node closes the least used ones and keeps its Idena peers: fewer connections use less data and battery. The default is 50, as on a computer; No limit keeps every connection. A low limit leaves too few for many peers: 20 needs Eco, 50 Eco or Normal.

The node takes the limit at its start.
The chain database holds the blockchain: the node writes to it at every block.

The IPFS database holds what the network uses to find content (which node has which flip, post or block). When nodes outside can reach the phone (a port open on the router), they store these records on it, and this database writes the most.

Default is 4 MiB, as on a computer. A higher level needs more RAM but writes less to the phone\'s storage (less wear, a little less work). If Android closes the node, choose a lower level. The node takes the size at its start.
The validation is running: restart the node after it.
The validation starts %1$s: the node may still be looking for peers then.

Nodes this node keeps as peers on top of its peer level, up to %1$d: a friend's desktop, your own computer. The node accepts them even when its slots are full, never drops them to make room, and connects again when the connection drops.

Share your node's code with the other person, and add theirs here. Both sides should add each other: the side that adds the other always accepts it. On mobile data no node can reach this phone, so the other node must be reachable (its router port open) for the two to connect.

resources.string: Open on %1$s for the phone\'s former address; the node moves it to the new one
Port %1$d on %2$s goes to another device (%3$s)

The port the node listens on for Idena nodes that connect to the phone (default %1$d). Behind one router each device needs its own port: a router forwards a port to one device only. Pick another one for a second phone or a computer on the same Wi-Fi, then open it in Router port.\n\nThe node takes the port at its start.

Opens the node's port (%1$d) on this Wi-Fi's router (UPnP), so that outside Idena nodes can connect to the phone. The router keeps it open until the end you choose, even if the phone leaves this Wi-Fi.

Open a port only if you know what it means: the node can then be reached from the internet.

Some routers announce themselves only every 15 minutes: finding one can take that long. Keep the screen on meanwhile, and check that the phone's battery settings do not stop the app in the background (on Samsung: Auto restart, in the battery settings).
Outside nodes can no longer connect to the phone. The peers connected at this moment drop within a minute; the node keeps looking for peers itself.
For how long? The router keeps it until then, also if the phone leaves this Wi-Fi.
